title: Six-class secp256k1 rho at 125.838547: one branch per group loop, 2^23 walks per batch, compares every 256th round

claims.statement: For a uniform full-production secp256k1 input Q=[x]P, the classical cold six-class negation-plus-GLV parallel Pollard-rho attack of proof.md and upstream-proof.md halts on every run with total work at most 2^125.838547 target-group-operation equivalents under classical-group-work-v2 (C=1000). It builds on bradcush's 02cc35d7 (125.838706) with three changes. First, each 128-walk group closes with one branch instead of SUBS and B.NE: TBZ on bit 26 of the pointer-array address in loop A (its test stub moved after RET) and pass1; in prod and pass 2, whose groups exceed TBZ's reach, CBNZ on the next pair's table pointer, loaded at the end of each pair and zero past the array (proof.md 2.5). Per walk: loop A 39.5078125 (43.0078125 in compare rounds, a hard row of 3.5), prod 171.5078125, pass 2 339.5078125. Second, n = 2^23 walks per batch share the round's fixed-work charge of 25,649 instructions: step 550.5234375 + 25649/2^23 = 550.5265 instructions. Third, the checkpoint is compared every 256th round and anchored every 8,192nd (proof.md 5.1). R = 2^26, kappa = 1.0001, h = 0.000048, p0 = 0.3900482, the reserve of 336 milli-units per walk (15 exits and one rare-path entry) and the doubling price step + 677 are kept; the zero-test re-run is its own 2^22-unit action. The declared run executes pass1, prod and pass2 on 139 production walks with 0 mismatches against big-integer affine secp256k1; both copies of loop A with 0 mismatches against big-integer dx and the address rule; arrive.s with 0 mismatches against the bit-exact model and the exact rule; and all 1,935 + 258 exit stubs on constructed inputs with 0 mismatches against the Python limb ports and big-integer differences, all with the production pointer-array layout. kappa = 1.0001 follows from the shipped hazard census: eleven walk rows, one of them at R = 2^26 (proof.md 5.2). Declared dependencies (proof.md section 6): 02cc35d7, 7dd2c482, 850e11fe, 886e6f54, a00774d8, c06f6691, 4ac17b66, 445f9a1c, cbea87bf, 4c8222cc, 0a1c5772, 5f1ae3ce, 4595bad7, 01488655, 2bd168b5, daf2c741, a9297fb0, 807e4bf5, b5de673a, 02feb284. Recovery probability is at least 0.39000009 > 0.39 (failure rows < 1.0103e-7 < 1.1e-7). Peak memory < 2^72 bytes; preprocessing capped at 2^59 units and included; no advice. Exact ledger (rounded up): S_ops = 1.0001*S0 < 2^126.6995024, phase 1 < 2^125.838387, hard extras < 2^110.850718, random extras < 2^97.8873, allowance < 2^112.2339, W_ledger < 2^125.8385465 <= 1000*2^125.838547 milli-units; Markov ratio at most 0.0000477897 (exact, rounded up; the declared run's float ledger, with its cycle rates rounded up, prints 0.0000477915) < 0.000048; certificate.py checks the claim and that 125.838546 fails, in exact arithmetic. No prior acceptance, review verdict or official score is a premise. This is an analytic heuristic bound, not a practical break.

experiments.purpose: Part A: production secp256k1 checks of the walk identities and the canonical-index rule; Part B: a scaled toy pipeline of the checkpoint-only walk (even-y key, per-trail phases, compares every 256th round) on subgroups of y^2=x^3+7 with node routing, a check that the old and the production compare rule reach the same endpoints, and an optional long-trail trap test (long_trails, not set in the declared run); kernels: Python limb ports of the field kernels against big integers, and the shipped loops (with rare exits on constructed inputs entering every stub), both copies of the fused pass (loop A: arrival and dx), emitter wrappers and arrival rows executed by an AArch64 interpreter (kernels/a64.py) against affine secp256k1, a bit-exact model and the exact canonical rule, with instruction counts and the ledger recomputed. The toy run does not meter production instructions or implement 2^23 concurrent walks.
